# 📐 PART 1: SCALABILITY SYSTEM

## 1.1 Scalability Philosophy

```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║  SCALABILITY DEFINITION (ISO/IEC 25010)                              ║
║                                                                       ║
║  WHAT:  The system's ability to handle growing amounts of work       ║
║         by adding resources without redesigning the system           ║
║                                                                       ║
║  WHY:   Rent & Lease grows: more landlords, more properties,        ║
║         more tenants, more transactions, more messages               ║
║                                                                       ║
║  WHEN:  Design for scale from Day 1 — retrofitting is 10x harder    ║
║                                                                       ║
║  WHERE: Every layer — DB, API, cache, queue, WebSocket, storage      ║
║                                                                       ║
║  HOW:   Horizontal + vertical scaling, caching, queuing,            ║
║         database optimization, CDN, connection pooling              ║
║                                                                       ║
║  TYPES OF SCALE:                                                      ║
║  → Vertical:   add more CPU/RAM to existing server                  ║
║  → Horizontal: add more servers behind a load balancer              ║
║  → Database:   read replicas, connection pooling, sharding          ║
║  → Cache:      Redis reducing DB load by 80%+                       ║
║  → Async:      Celery offloading heavy tasks from request cycle     ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

---

## 1.2 Database Scalability

```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║  DATABASE SCALABILITY — COMPLETE SPECIFICATION                        ║
║  Reference: "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" Ch. 3-6          ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                       ║
║  CURRENT STATE (XAMPP/MySQL):                                        ║
║  → Single MySQL instance via XAMPP                                  ║
║  → Adequate for: 0-10,000 records                                   ║
║  → Bottleneck at: heavy read queries, concurrent writes             ║
║                                                                       ║
║  SCALE PATH (Growth Stages):                                         ║
║                                                                       ║
║  STAGE 1 (0-1,000 landlords):                                       ║
║  → XAMPP MySQL — current setup                                      ║
║  → Proper indexing on all foreign keys and filter fields            ║
║  → Connection pooling: CONN_MAX_AGE=60 in Django settings           ║
║  → Query optimization: select_related() and prefetch_related()     ║
║  → No N+1 queries allowed anywhere                                  ║
║                                                                       ║
║  STAGE 2 (1,000-10,000 landlords):                                  ║
║  → Move to dedicated MySQL server (separate from app server)        ║
║  → Add MySQL read replica for Analytics and Dashboard queries       ║
║  → Implement Redis caching for non-financial read queries           ║
║  → Add database connection pooling (PgBouncer or ProxySQL)         ║
║                                                                       ║
║  STAGE 3 (10,000+ landlords):                                       ║
║  → MySQL Cluster or migration to PostgreSQL                         ║
║  → Horizontal read replicas (2-5 replicas)                         ║
║  → Write to primary, read from replicas                             ║
║  → Partition large tables (audit_logs, notifications by date)       ║
║                                                                       ║
║  DATABASE INDEXING RULES (MANDATORY NOW):                            ║
║                                                                       ║
║  TABLE: users                                                        ║
║  → INDEX: email (unique)                                            ║
║  → INDEX: role, is_active                                           ║
║  → INDEX: email, role (composite)                                   ║
║                                                                       ║
║  TABLE: properties                                                   ║
║  → INDEX: landlord_id                                               ║
║  → INDEX: landlord_id, is_deleted                                   ║
║  → INDEX: landlord_id, status                                       ║
║                                                                       ║
║  TABLE: leases                                                       ║
║  → INDEX: property_id                                               ║
║  → INDEX: tenant_id                                                 ║
║  → INDEX: status                                                    ║
║  → INDEX: start_date, end_date (composite — for overlap check)     ║
║  → INDEX: property_id, status, start_date, end_date (composite)    ║
║                                                                       ║
║  TABLE: invoices                                                     ║
║  → INDEX: lease_id                                                  ║
║  → INDEX: status                                                    ║
║  → INDEX: due_date                                                  ║
║  → INDEX: due_date, status (composite — for Celery tasks)          ║
║                                                                       ║
║  TABLE: audit_logs                                                   ║
║  → INDEX: user_id                                                   ║
║  → INDEX: timestamp (for time-range queries)                        ║
║  → INDEX: resource, resource_id (for object history)               ║
║  → PARTITION BY RANGE (timestamp) — monthly partitions             ║
║                                                                       ║
║  TABLE: messages (Chat)                                             ║
║  → INDEX: conversation_id                                           ║
║  → INDEX: sender_id                                                 ║
║  → INDEX: created_at                                                ║
║  → PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at) — monthly partitions            ║
║                                                                       ║
║  TABLE: notifications                                               ║
║  → INDEX: recipient_id, is_read                                    ║
║  → INDEX: recipient_id, created_at                                  ║
║  → PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at) — monthly partitions            ║
║                                                                       ║
║  QUERY OPTIMIZATION RULES:                                           ║
║                                                                       ║
║  → NEVER: queryset without a filter (no full table scans)          ║
║  → ALWAYS: use select_related() for ForeignKey traversal           ║
║  → ALWAYS: use prefetch_related() for reverse FK and M2M           ║
║  → ALWAYS: use only() to select needed columns                     ║
║  → ALWAYS: use values() or values_list() for read-only reporting   ║
║  → ALWAYS: paginate — never return unlimited records               ║
║  → NEVER: filter inside a Python loop (N+1 problem)                ║
║  → ALWAYS: use annotate() for computed fields instead of Python    ║
║  → ALWAYS: use bulk_create() and bulk_update() for batch ops       ║
║                                                                       ║
║  AI CHECK: Verify no N+1 queries in any view or serializer          ║
║  AI CHECK: Verify select_related on all FK traversals               ║
║  AI CHECK: Verify all filter columns have DB indexes                ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

## 1.3 Application Scalability

```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║  APPLICATION SCALABILITY                                              ║
║  Reference: 12-Factor App, "Release It!" by Nygard                  ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                       ║
║  12-FACTOR APP COMPLIANCE (MANDATORY):                               ║
║                                                                       ║
║  Factor 1: CODEBASE                                                  ║
║  → One codebase tracked in Git                                      ║
║  → Multiple deploys (dev, staging, production)                      ║
║  → NEVER commit: .env, secrets, credentials, debug code            ║
║  → ALWAYS: .gitignore covers venv, __pycache__, .env, media/       ║
║                                                                       ║
║  Factor 2: DEPENDENCIES                                              ║
║  → All dependencies in requirements.txt with pinned versions        ║
║  → NEVER rely on system-wide packages                               ║
║  → Use virtual environment (venv) — already in use                 ║
║  → Split: requirements/base.txt, dev.txt, production.txt           ║
║                                                                       ║
║  Factor 3: CONFIG                                                    ║
║  → ALL config in environment variables via .env + python-decouple  ║
║  → NEVER: SECRET_KEY, DB_PASSWORD, JWT_SECRET in code              ║
║  → NEVER: DEBUG=True in production                                  ║
║  → Config that changes per environment: in .env only               ║
║                                                                       ║
║  Factor 4: BACKING SERVICES                                          ║
║  → MySQL, Redis, SMTP treated as attached resources                 ║
║  → Connection strings in environment variables                      ║
║  → Can swap MySQL for another DB without code changes               ║
║                                                                       ║
║  Factor 5: BUILD, RELEASE, RUN                                      ║
║  → Build: collect static, compile assets                            ║
║  → Release: combine build with config                               ║
║  → Run: start Daphne, Celery worker, Celery beat                   ║
║  → These stages are strictly separated                              ║
║                                                                       ║
║  Factor 6: PROCESSES                                                 ║
║  → App is stateless — no in-memory session state                   ║
║  → Sessions stored in DB (already configured)                       ║
║  → Files stored externally — not on app server                     ║
║  → Multiple app instances can run simultaneously                    ║
║                                                                       ║
║  Factor 7: PORT BINDING                                              ║
║  → App is self-contained — exports service via port                ║
║  → Daphne binds to port 8000                                        ║
║  → Nginx proxies in front of Daphne                                 ║
║                                                                       ║
║  Factor 8: CONCURRENCY                                               ║
║  → Scale out via process model (multiple Daphne workers)            ║
║  → Celery workers scale independently of web workers               ║
║  → Each process type scales based on demand                        ║
║                                                                       ║
║  Factor 9: DISPOSABILITY                                             ║
║  → Fast startup — app ready in < 10 seconds                        ║
║  → Graceful shutdown — finish in-flight requests before exit       ║
║  → Celery workers: graceful shutdown completes current task        ║
║                                                                       ║
║  Factor 10: DEV/PROD PARITY                                         ║
║  → Dev environment mirrors production as closely as possible        ║
║  → Same MySQL version in dev and production                        ║
║  → Same Redis version in dev and production                        ║
║  → Use Docker Compose for local parity (future improvement)        ║
║                                                                       ║
║  Factor 11: LOGS                                                     ║
║  → App writes logs to stdout/stderr                                 ║
║  → Log aggregator captures and stores (file-based now)              ║
║  → Structured JSON logging for machine parsing                     ║
║  → Log levels: DEBUG (dev only), INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL    ║
║                                                                       ║
║  Factor 12: ADMIN PROCESSES                                          ║
║  → DB migrations: python manage.py migrate                          ║
║  → Data fixes: python manage.py shell or custom command            ║
║  → Run as one-off processes in same environment as app             ║
║                                                                       ║
║  AI CHECK: Verify no secrets in codebase                            ║
║  AI CHECK: Verify no stateful in-memory data in views               ║
║  AI CHECK: Verify all config comes from environment                 ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

## 1.4 Caching Scalability

```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║  CACHING STRATEGY                                                     ║
║  Reference: "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" Ch. 4            ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                       ║
║  CACHE LAYERS (Redis — already installed):                           ║
║                                                                       ║
║  LAYER 1: Django Cache Framework (Redis backend)                    ║
║  → Cache expensive read queries                                     ║
║  → Cache computed dashboard metrics (5 min TTL)                    ║
║  → Cache analytics aggregates (1 hour TTL)                         ║
║  → NEVER cache: financial totals, auth data, sensitive PII          ║
║                                                                       ║
║  LAYER 2: Django Template Fragment Caching                          ║
║  → Cache static sidebar (rarely changes)                            ║
║  → Cache property grid cards (invalidate on property change)        ║
║  → NEVER cache: user-specific financial data                        ║
║                                                                       ║
║  LAYER 3: HTTP Response Caching                                     ║
║  → Cache-Control headers for static assets                          ║
║  → NEVER cache: authenticated API responses                         ║
║  → Always: Cache-Control: no-store for authenticated pages         ║
║                                                                       ║
║  CACHE INVALIDATION RULES (Cache Invalidation is Hard):             ║
║                                                                       ║
║  → Property changes → invalidate property grid cache               ║
║  → Lease status change → invalidate dashboard metrics cache        ║
║  → Invoice payment → invalidate financial metrics cache            ║
║  → Rule: invalidate on WRITE, serve stale on READ                  ║
║  → Rule: use cache versioning, not key deletion                    ║
║  → Rule: cache keys include user_id to prevent data leakage        ║
║                                                                       ║
║  CACHE KEY NAMING CONVENTION:                                        ║
║  → Format: {app}:{resource}:{user_id}:{params_hash}               ║
║  → Example: dashboard:metrics:usr_abc123:v2                        ║
║  → NEVER: cache key contains sensitive data                        ║
║  → ALWAYS: cache key is scoped to specific user                    ║
║                                                                       ║
║  WHAT MUST NEVER BE CACHED:                                          ║
║  → Real-time financial totals (invoice amounts)                    ║
║  → Authentication tokens or session data                           ║
║  → Personally Identifiable Information (PII)                        ║
║  → Security-related data (permissions, roles)                      ║
║  → Data that must be immediately consistent (payments)              ║
║                                                                       ║
║  AI CHECK: Verify cache keys include user_id                        ║
║  AI CHECK: Verify financial data is NOT cached                      ║
║  AI CHECK: Verify cache invalidation on every write operation       ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

## 1.5 Async & Queue Scalability

```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║  CELERY TASK QUEUE SCALABILITY                                        ║
║  Reference: "Release It!" — Stability Patterns                       ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                       ║
║  TASK QUEUE PRINCIPLES:                                              ║
║                                                                       ║
║  PRINCIPLE 1: OFFLOAD EVERYTHING HEAVY                              ║
║  → Anything > 200ms belongs in a Celery task                       ║
║  → Email sending: always async (never block HTTP response)         ║
║  → PDF generation: always async                                     ║
║  → Invoice generation: always async                                 ║
║  → Late fee calculation: always async                               ║
║  → Analytics aggregation: always async (cached result)             ║
║  → File processing: always async                                    ║
║  → Notification broadcasting: always async                         ║
║                                                                       ║
║  PRINCIPLE 2: TASK IDEMPOTENCY                                      ║
║  → Every Celery task MUST be safe to run multiple times            ║
║  → Use unique constraints in DB to prevent duplicate records       ║
║  → Check-before-act: verify record doesn't exist before creating  ║
║  → Invoice task: check if invoice for month already exists first   ║
║  → Late fee task: check if fee already applied before applying    ║
║                                                                       ║
║  PRINCIPLE 3: TASK ISOLATION                                        ║
║  → Tasks MUST NOT depend on in-memory state from the web process  ║
║  → Tasks receive only IDs — they fetch fresh data from DB         ║
║  → NEVER pass entire model objects to tasks — only PKs            ║
║  → Tasks are self-contained units of work                          ║
║                                                                       ║
║  PRINCIPLE 4: TASK FAILURE HANDLING                                 ║
║  → Every task has retry logic with exponential backoff             ║
║  → Max retries: 3 attempts                                         ║
║  → Failed tasks logged to error log with full context             ║
║  → Dead letter queue for permanently failed tasks                  ║
║  → Alerting when task failure rate exceeds threshold               ║
║                                                                       ║
║  PRINCIPLE 5: TASK PRIORITIZATION                                   ║
║  → HIGH priority queue: real-time notifications, emails           ║
║  → MEDIUM priority queue: invoice generation, fee calculation     ║
║  → LOW priority queue: reports, analytics, PDF generation         ║
║  → Different Celery workers can handle different queues            ║
║                                                                       ║
║  CELERY BEAT SCHEDULED TASKS (MAINTENANCE SCHEDULE):               ║
║                                                                       ║
║  00:01 DAILY:                                                        ║
║  → lease_status_transition (PENDING→ACTIVE→EXPIRED)               ║
║  → late_fee_application (overdue invoices)                         ║
║  → expiry_warning_notifications (60, 14, 7 days)                  ║
║  → session_cleanup (expired sessions)                              ║
║                                                                       ║
║  00:01 MONTHLY (1st):                                               ║
║  → monthly_invoice_generation (all active leases)                  ║
║  → monthly_financial_report_email (if enabled)                     ║
║  → monthly_analytics_cache_warmup                                   ║
║                                                                       ║
║  00:01 WEEKLY (Sunday):                                             ║
║  → old_notification_archival (>1 year general notifications)       ║
║  → temporary_file_cleanup (orphaned uploads)                       ║
║                                                                       ║
║  AI CHECK: Verify tasks receive only PKs not model objects          ║
║  AI CHECK: Verify every task has retry logic                        ║
║  AI CHECK: Verify invoice/fee tasks check for duplicates first      ║
║  AI CHECK: Verify task names are hardcoded (Reminder page rule)    ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

# 🌱 PART 2: SUSTAINABILITY SYSTEM

```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║  SUSTAINABILITY FRAMEWORK                                             ║
║  Reference: ISO/IEC 25010 — Maintainability + Portability           ║
║  Reference: "Software Engineering at Google" — Long-term Health     ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                       ║
║  SUSTAINABILITY DEFINITION:                                          ║
║  The system's ability to continue delivering value over time        ║
║  without accumulating technical debt that makes change painful      ║
║                                                                       ║
║  5 DIMENSIONS OF SUSTAINABILITY:                                     ║
║  1. Code Sustainability    → Clean, readable, testable code         ║
║  2. Data Sustainability    → Data integrity over time               ║
║  3. Dependency Sustainab.  → No abandoned or vulnerable packages    ║
║  4. Team Sustainability    → Knowledge not siloed in one person     ║
║  5. Business Sustainability→ System evolves with business needs     ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

## 2.1 Code Sustainability

```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║  CODE SUSTAINABILITY PRINCIPLES                                       ║
║  Reference: "Clean Architecture" + "A Philosophy of Software Design" ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                       ║
║  PRINCIPLE 1: SINGLE RESPONSIBILITY                                  ║
║  → Every class, function, module has ONE reason to change           ║
║  → Views: only handle HTTP request/response                         ║
║  → Serializers: only handle data validation and transformation      ║
║  → Business rules: only in dedicated business logic classes         ║
║  → Models: only data definition and simple data access              ║
║  → Celery tasks: only task orchestration                            ║
║  → Middleware: only cross-cutting concerns                          ║
║                                                                       ║
║  CHECK: LeaseBusinessRules in dedicated file, not in views          ║
║  CHECK: FileUploadSecurity in dedicated file, not in models         ║
║  CHECK: InvoiceGenerator class, not inline in view                 ║
║                                                                       ║
║  PRINCIPLE 2: DON'T REPEAT YOURSELF (DRY)                          ║
║  → Business rules defined once — referenced everywhere              ║
║  → Late fee rate: ONE constant, used everywhere                    ║
║  → Grace period: ONE constant, used everywhere                     ║
║  → Validation logic: ONE serializer field validator, reused        ║
║  → Template fragments: ONE include, used across all 14 pages       ║
║  → Sidebar: ONE template, included in all layout files             ║
║                                                                       ║
║  ANTI-PATTERNS TO PREVENT:                                           ║
║  → Magic numbers: 5 (grace days) appears in 3 files               ║
║     FIX: GRACE_PERIOD_DAYS = 5 in constants.py, imported everywhere║
║  → Copy-paste code: same validation in view AND serializer         ║
║     FIX: validation in serializer only — view uses serializer      ║
║  → Duplicated SQL: same query in view and in Celery task           ║
║     FIX: shared queryset method on Model Manager                   ║
║                                                                       ║
║  PRINCIPLE 3: OPEN/CLOSED PRINCIPLE                                 ║
║  → Open for extension, closed for modification                     ║
║  → Adding new notification type: add to TYPE_CHOICES, no rewrite  ║
║  → Adding new automation type: add to AUTOMATION_TYPES, no rewrite ║
║  → Adding new property type: add to TYPE_CHOICES, no rewrite      ║
║  → New business rule: add new method, don't change existing ones  ║
║                                                                       ║
║  PRINCIPLE 4: DEPENDENCY INVERSION                                  ║
║  → High-level modules (views) don't depend on low-level (queries)  ║
║  → Views depend on service layer abstractions                      ║
║  → Service layer depends on model abstractions                     ║
║  → Makes testing possible without DB                               ║
║                                                                       ║
║  LAYERED ARCHITECTURE (MANDATORY):                                   ║
║                                                                       ║
║  REQUEST                                                             ║
║  ↓                                                                   ║
║  MIDDLEWARE (auth, rate limit, headers, audit)                      ║
║  ↓                                                                   ║
║  VIEW / API ENDPOINT (HTTP handling only)                           ║
║  ↓                                                                   ║
║  SERIALIZER (validation + transformation)                           ║
║  ↓                                                                   ║
║  BUSINESS LOGIC LAYER (rules, laws, logic)                          ║
║  ↓                                                                   ║
║  SERVICE LAYER (DB queries via Model Managers)                      ║
║  ↓                                                                   ║
║  MODEL LAYER (data definitions + constraints)                       ║
║  ↓                                                                   ║
║  DATABASE (MySQL via XAMPP)                                          ║
║                                                                       ║
║  RULE: Layers only communicate with adjacent layers                 ║
║  RULE: Views NEVER touch DB directly — always via service layer    ║
║  RULE: Business logic NEVER in templates or JS                     ║
║  RULE: All business rules ONLY on server — never on client         ║
║                                                                       ║
║  AI CHECK: Verify views don't contain business logic                ║
║  AI CHECK: Verify no ORM queries in templates                       ║
║  AI CHECK: Verify business constants are in constants.py            ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

## 2.2 Dependency Sustainability

```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║  DEPENDENCY MANAGEMENT SUSTAINABILITY                                 ║
║  Reference: "The Pragmatic Programmer" — Dependency Management      ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                       ║
║  DEPENDENCY RULES:                                                   ║
║                                                                       ║
║  RULE 1: PIN ALL VERSIONS                                            ║
║  → requirements.txt must pin exact versions                         ║
║  → BAD:  django>=4.0                                                ║
║  → GOOD: django==4.2.30                                             ║

║  → Monthly: check PyPI for deprecated packages                     ║
║  → On CVE alert: patch within 48 hours (critical) 1 week (high)   ║
║                                                                       ║

║  → Prefer: Django-ecosystem packages over generic Python           ║
║  → Avoid: packages with single maintainer and no backup            ║
║                                                                       ║
║  APPROVED PACKAGE LIST (CURRENT):                                    ║
║                                                                       ║
║  CORE:                                                               ║
║  → django==4.2.30            (LTS — supported until April 2026)   ║

║  SECURITY:                                                           ║

║  → django-csp                (Content Security Policy)             ║

║                                                                       ║
║  DATABASE:                                                           ║
║  → mysqlclient               (MySQL connector)                     ║

║                                                                       ║

# ⚠️ PART 3: RISK MANAGEMENT SYSTEM

## 3.1 Risk Framework

```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║  RISK MANAGEMENT FRAMEWORK                                            ║
║  Reference: ISO 31000:2018 — Risk Management                        ║
║  Reference: "Release It!" — Stability Patterns                      ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                       ║
║  RISK DEFINITION:                                                    ║
║  Risk = Probability × Impact                                         ║
║                                                                       ║
║  RISK LEVELS:                                                        ║
║  CRITICAL: Immediate threat to data, money, or system availability  ║
║  HIGH:     Significant impact on business operations                ║
║  MEDIUM:   Noticeable degradation of service or data quality        ║
║  LOW:      Minor inconvenience, easily recoverable                  ║
║                                                                       ║
║  RISK CATEGORIES:                                                    ║
║  1. Security Risks        → Data breach, unauthorized access       ║
║  2. Data Risks            → Loss, corruption, inconsistency        ║
║  3. Performance Risks     → Slow response, timeouts, crashes       ║
║  4. Availability Risks    → Downtime, service interruption         ║
║  5. Compliance Risks      → Legal violations, regulatory breaches  ║
║  6. Dependency Risks      → Third-party failures, deprecations     ║
║  7. Human Risks           → Developer errors, knowledge loss       ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

## 3.2 Risk Register

```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║  RISK REGISTER — COMPLETE                                             ║
╠══════════╦═══════════╦══════════╦═══════════════════════════════════╣
║  RISK ID ║ SEVERITY  ║ CATEGORY ║ DESCRIPTION + MITIGATION          ║
╠══════════╬═══════════╬══════════╬═══════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                       ║
║  RISK-01: MYSQL DATA LOSS (XAMPP)                                    ║
║  Severity:   CRITICAL                                                ║
║  Category:   Data Risk                                               ║
║  Probability:Medium (XAMPP is not production-grade)                 ║
║  Impact:     CRITICAL — all landlord and tenant data lost           ║
║                                                                       ║
║  WHAT:  XAMPP MySQL crashes or disk failure causes data loss        ║
║  WHEN:  Any time — hardware failure, power loss, corrupt write      ║
║  WHERE: MySQL data directory under XAMPP                            ║
║  WHY:   XAMPP has no built-in backup or replication                ║
║  HOW TO MITIGATE:                                                    ║
║  → IMMEDIATE: Automated daily DB backup to separate location       ║
║  → Script: mysqldump daily at 02:00, compress, store 30 days       ║
║  → Weekly: backup to external storage (USB or cloud)               ║
║  → Test: monthly restore drill — verify backup is restorable       ║
║  → Future: migrate to dedicated MySQL server with replication      ║
║                                                                       ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                       ║
║  RISK-02: REDIS FAILURE                                              ║
║  Severity:   HIGH                                                    ║
║  Category:   Availability Risk                                       ║
║  Probability:Medium (Redis has no persistence by default)           ║
║  Impact:     HIGH — WebSocket breaks, Celery stops, cache lost     ║
║                                                                       ║
║  WHAT:  Redis process crashes or is restarted                      ║
║  WHEN:  System restart, memory exhaustion, crash                   ║
║  WHERE: Redis server (currently same machine as app)               ║
║  HOW TO MITIGATE:                                                    ║
║  → Enable Redis RDB persistence (dump.rdb every 60 seconds)       ║
║  → Enable Redis AOF persistence (appendonly yes)                   ║
║  → Set Redis maxmemory-policy: allkeys-lru                         ║
║  → Django gracefully falls back if cache unavailable               ║
║  → Celery retries tasks if Redis disconnects                       ║
║  → Monitor Redis memory usage — alert at 80%                       ║
║                                                                       ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                       ║
║  RISK-03: CELERY TASK FAILURE — MISSED INVOICES                      ║
║  Severity:   CRITICAL                                                ║
║  Category:   Data Risk + Compliance Risk                            ║
║  Probability:Low-Medium                                              ║
║  Impact:     CRITICAL — invoices not generated, revenue not tracked ║
║                                                                       ║
║  WHAT:  Monthly invoice Celery task fails silently                  ║
║  WHEN:  1st of month at 00:01                                       ║
║  WHY:   Task error, Redis down, DB connection issue                 ║
║  HOW TO MITIGATE:                                                    ║
║  → Task has retry logic: 3 retries with 5-minute backoff           ║
║  → Task is idempotent: safe to run multiple times (checks exist)  ║
║  → After all retries fail: email alert to admin                    ║
║  → Daily check task: verify invoice count matches active leases   ║
║  → If mismatch: alert admin to manually trigger invoice generation ║
║  → Log all task runs: success, fail, count processed, duration    ║
║                                                                       ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                       ║
║  RISK-04: SQL INJECTION ATTACK                                        ║
║  Severity:   CRITICAL                                                ║
║  Category:   Security Risk                                           ║
║  Probability:Low (ORM used) but CRITICAL if occurs                  ║
║  Impact:     CRITICAL — all data exposed, modified, or deleted      ║
║                                                                       ║
║  HOW TO MITIGATE:                                                    ║
║  → ONLY Django ORM for all queries (Section A checklist)           ║
║  → Any raw SQL uses parameterized form (cursor.execute + params)   ║
║  → DB user has least privilege (no DROP, no CREATE)                ║
║  → Regular security audits with bandit tool                        ║
║  → AI security check on every code review (mandatory)             ║
║                                                                       ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                       ║
║  RISK-05: CROSS-SITE SCRIPTING (XSS) IN CHAT                        ║
║  Severity:   CRITICAL                                                ║
║  Category:   Security Risk                                           ║
║  Probability:Medium (user-generated content in real-time)           ║
║  Impact:     CRITICAL — session hijack, data theft                  ║
║                                                                       ║
║  HOW TO MITIGATE:                                                    ║
║  → ALL message rendering uses textContent (NEVER innerHTML)        ║
║  → Server sanitizes before DB save AND before broadcast            ║
║  → CSP blocks inline scripts even if XSS succeeds                 ║
║  → Regular penetration testing on Chat endpoint                    ║
║                                                                       ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                       ║
║  RISK-06: CONCURRENT LEASE CREATION (RACE CONDITION)                 ║
║  Severity:   HIGH                                                    ║
║  Category:   Data Risk + Compliance Risk                            ║
║  Probability:Low but possible                                        ║
║  Impact:     HIGH — two active leases on same unit (illegal)        ║
║                                                                       ║
║  WHAT:  Two requests create lease on same unit simultaneously       ║
║  WHEN:  Concurrent API calls (automated or manual)                  ║
║  HOW TO MITIGATE:                                                    ║
║  → Use SELECT FOR UPDATE on unit row during lease creation         ║
║  → Wrap entire lease creation in atomic transaction                ║
║  → Database unique constraint: unit + active status + date range  ║
║  → If race condition detected: second request gets 409 Conflict    ║
║  → Test with concurrent requests in QA                             ║
║                                                                       ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                       ║
║  RISK-07: LATE FEE APPLIED TWICE (DUPLICATE TASK)                   ║
║  Severity:   HIGH                                                    ║
║  Category:   Data Risk + Compliance Risk                            ║
║  Probability:Low                                                     ║
║  Impact:     HIGH — overcharged tenants, legal liability            ║
║                                                                       ║
║  HOW TO MITIGATE:                                                    ║
║  → Invoice model has boolean: late_fee_applied (default False)     ║
║  → Celery task checks late_fee_applied before applying            ║
║  → DB unique constraint: one late fee record per invoice           ║
║  → Task is fully idempotent                                         ║
║                                                                       ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                       ║
║  RISK-08: UNAUTHORIZED DATA ACCESS (IDOR)                            ║
║  Severity:   CRITICAL                                                ║
║  Category:   Security Risk                                           ║
║  Probability:Medium (common attack)                                  ║
║  Impact:     CRITICAL — one landlord accesses another's data        ║
║                                                                       ║
║  HOW TO MITIGATE:                                                    ║
║  → Every queryset filtered by landlord=request.user                 ║
║  → Object-level permission check on detail views                   ║
║  → Return 404 (not 403) for unauthorized objects                   ║
║  → IDORProtectionMiddleware monitors for probing patterns          ║
║  → UUID primary keys prevent sequential enumeration                ║
║                                                                       ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                       ║
║  RISK-09: FILE UPLOAD ATTACK                                         ║
║  Severity:   CRITICAL                                                ║
║  Category:   Security Risk                                           ║
║  Probability:Medium (common attack vector)                           ║
║  Impact:     CRITICAL — remote code execution if .php/.exe uploaded ║
║                                                                       ║
║  HOW TO MITIGATE:                                                    ║
║  → MIME type verified with python-magic (reads file header bytes)  ║
║  → Extension validated against allowlist                           ║
║  → File stored with UUID name (not original name)                  ║
║  → Files stored OUTSIDE web root (no direct URL access)            ║
║  → Max file size enforced server-side                              ║
║  → Nginx configured to not execute files in media directory        ║
║                                                                       ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                       ║
║  RISK-10: DJANGO LTS END OF LIFE                                     ║
║  Severity:   HIGH                                                    ║
║  Category:   Dependency Risk                                         ║
║  Probability:Certain (Django 4.2 LTS ends April 2026)              ║
║  Impact:     HIGH — no security patches for known CVEs              ║
║                                                                       ║
║  HOW TO MITIGATE:                                                    ║
║  → Plan Django 5.x migration by Q1 2026                            ║
║  → Test migration in staging environment                            ║
║  → Review deprecation warnings with each minor release             ║
║  → Assign migration to sprint before EOL date                     ║
║                                                                       ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                       ║
║  RISK-11: SESSION HIJACKING VIA TOKEN THEFT                          ║
║  Severity:   CRITICAL                                                ║
║  Category:   Security Risk                                           ║
║  Probability:Low-Medium                                              ║
║  Impact:     CRITICAL — attacker impersonates landlord              ║
║                                                                       ║
║  HOW TO MITIGATE:                                                    ║
║  → JWT access token: 15 minutes lifetime (short window)            ║
║  → Refresh token: HttpOnly cookie (not accessible to JS)           ║
║  → Rotate refresh token on every use                               ║
║  → Blacklist refresh tokens on logout                              ║
║  → Detect: same token used from different IPs → force logout       ║
║  → HTTPS only (HSTS enforced)                                       ║
║                                                                       ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                       ║
║  RISK-12: KNOWLEDGE LOSS (BUS FACTOR = 1)                           ║
║  Severity:   HIGH                                                    ║
║  Category:   Human Risk                                              ║
║  Probability:Medium                                                  ║
║  Impact:     HIGH — system cannot be maintained or extended         ║
║                                                                       ║
║  HOW TO MITIGATE:                                                    ║
║  → Comprehensive documentation in docs/ folder                     ║
║  → README.md: setup, run, deploy instructions                      ║
║  → ARCHITECTURE.md: system design decisions                        ║
║  → BUSINESS_RULES.md: all business logic documented               ║
║  → SECURITY_CHECKLIST.md: all security controls documented        ║
║  → API documentation via drf-spectacular (auto-generated)          ║
║  → Code comments on non-obvious logic                              ║
║  → Docstrings on all business logic classes and methods            ║
║                                                                       ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

## 3.3 Stability Patterns

```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║  STABILITY PATTERNS                                                   ║
║  Reference: "Release It!" — Chapter 4 Stability Antipatterns        ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                       ║
║  PATTERN 1: TIMEOUTS                                                 ║
║  → Every external call MUST have a timeout                          ║
║  → DB connection timeout: 10 seconds                                ║
║  → DB read timeout: 30 seconds                                      ║
║  → Email SMTP timeout: 10 seconds (handled by Celery, not request) ║
║  → Redis connection timeout: 5 seconds                              ║
║  → HTTP requests (if any) timeout: 10 seconds                      ║
║  → WHY: Without timeouts, one slow dependency hangs entire system  ║
║                                                                       ║
║  PATTERN 2: CIRCUIT BREAKER                                         ║
║  → Email sending: if SMTP fails 5 times, stop trying for 10 min   ║
║  → Redis: if Redis unreachable, cache falls back to DB             ║
║  → External API: if 3rd party fails, return cached result          ║
║  → WHY: Prevents cascade failures from propagating                 ║
║                                                                       ║
║  PATTERN 3: BULKHEADS                                               ║
║  → Web workers isolated from Celery workers                         ║
║  → Chat WebSocket connections isolated from REST API               ║
║  → Analytics queries on read replica (isolated from write path)   ║
║  → WHY: Failure in one area doesn't cascade to others             ║
║                                                                       ║
║  PATTERN 4: FAIL FAST                                               ║
║  → Validate ALL input at API boundary — reject early               ║
║  → Check permissions at middleware — reject before view runs       ║
║  → Check business rules before any DB write                        ║
║  → WHY: Find problems early, before they corrupt data              ║
║                                                                       ║
║  PATTERN 5: HANDSHAKING                                             ║
║  → Health check endpoint: /health/ returns system status           ║
║  → Checks: DB connected, Redis connected, Celery running           ║
║  → Load balancer uses health check before routing traffic          ║
║  → App refuses traffic if not healthy                              ║
║                                                                       ║
║  ANTI-PATTERNS TO PREVENT:                                           ║
║                                                                       ║
║  → INTEGRATION POINTS WITHOUT TIMEOUT: Every DB/Redis call         ║
║    must have timeout — already set in DATABASES OPTIONS            ║
║  → UNBOUNDED RESULT SETS: Every queryset has pagination            ║
║    limit — no endpoint returns unlimited rows                      ║
║  → CASCADING FAILURES: Celery queue depth limited                  ║
║    to prevent memory exhaustion                                    ║
║  → SLOW RESPONSES: Any operation > 200ms moved to Celery           ║
║  → MEMORY LEAKS: No unbounded in-memory collections               ║
║    in long-running processes                                       ║
║                                                                       ║
║  AI CHECK: Verify all DB connection options have timeout set        ║
║  AI CHECK: Verify all list views have pagination enforced           ║
║  AI CHECK: Verify heavy operations are in Celery tasks             ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

# 🔧 PART 4: MAINTAINABILITY SYSTEM

## 4.1 Code Quality Standards

```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║  CODE QUALITY STANDARDS                                               ║
║  Reference: "Refactoring" Fowler + "Clean Code" Martin              ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                       ║
║  NAMING CONVENTIONS (MANDATORY):                                     ║
║                                                                       ║
║  Python:                                                             ║
║  → Classes:          PascalCase     (LeaseBusinessRules)            ║
║  → Functions:        snake_case     (calculate_late_fee)            ║
║  → Variables:        snake_case     (monthly_rent)                  ║
║  → Constants:        UPPER_SNAKE    (LATE_FEE_PERCENTAGE)           ║
║  → Private methods:  _snake_case    (_validate_dates)               ║
║  → Private attrs:    __snake_case   (__csrf_token)                  ║
║  → Files:            snake_case     (business_rules.py)             ║
║  → Django apps:      snake_case     (apps/leases/)                  ║
║                                                                       ║
║  Django specifics:                                                   ║
║  → URL names:        app:action     (landlord:lease-list)           ║
║  → Template names:   app/page.html (landlord/leases.html)          ║
║  → Model names:      Singular       (Lease not Leases)             ║
║  → Manager names:    DescriptiveManager (ActiveLeaseManager)        ║
║                                                                       ║
║  JavaScript:                                                         ║
║  → Classes:          PascalCase     (SecureHTTP)                   ║
║  → Functions:        camelCase      (calculateLateFee)             ║
║  → Variables:        camelCase      (monthlyRent)                  ║
║  → Constants:        UPPER_SNAKE    (MAX_MESSAGE_LENGTH)            ║
║  → Private:         #prefix         (#csrfToken)                   ║
║                                                                       ║
║  CSS:                                                                ║
║  → Components:       BEM notation   (.card__header--active)        ║
║  → Custom props:     --category-name (--color-primary)             ║
║  → JS hooks:         data-* attrs   (data-action="submit")         ║
║  → Utility classes:  descriptive    (.animate-fade-up)             ║
║                                                                       ║
║  FUNCTION/METHOD LENGTH RULES:                                       ║
║  → Maximum: 20 lines per function (Uncle Bob's rule)               ║
║  → If > 20 lines: extract to smaller functions                     ║
║  → One function = one job                                           ║
║  → Deeply nested code (>3 levels): extract to functions            ║
║                                                                       ║
║  COMMENT RULES:                                                      ║
║  → WHY comments: explain business reason, not what code does       ║
║  → WHAT comments: only for non-obvious algorithms                  ║
║  → BAD: # increment i by 1 → i += 1                               ║
║  → GOOD: # Grace period: 5 days per Landlord and Tenant Act        ║
║  → Docstrings: on all classes and public methods                   ║
║  → TODO format: # TODO(author): description + ticket number        ║
║                                                                       ║
║  AI CHECK: Verify function length < 20 lines                        ║
║  AI CHECK: Verify naming conventions followed                       ║
║  AI CHECK: Verify business constants extracted to constants.py      ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

## 4.3 Testing Strategy

```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║  TESTING STRATEGY                                                     ║
║  Reference: "Accelerate" — DORA Metrics, Test Automation            ║
║  Reference: Google Testing Blog — Test Pyramid                      ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                       ║
║  TEST PYRAMID:                                                       ║
║                                                                       ║
║                 /\                                                   ║
║                /  \                                                  ║
║               / E2E\  (5%) — Browser automation, full flow tests    ║
║              /──────\                                                ║
║             /Integrat\  (25%) — API tests, DB tests, Celery tests   ║
║            /──────────\                                              ║
║           /  Unit Tests\  (70%) — Business logic, validators, utils ║
║          /──────────────\                                            ║
║                                                                       ║
║  UNIT TESTS (MANDATORY):                                             ║
║                                                                       ║
║  → Test every business rule in business_rules.py                   ║
║  → Test every serializer validator                                  ║
║  → Test every utility function                                      ║
║  → Test every permission class                                      ║
║  → NO database — use mocks                                          ║
║  → Run in: < 10 seconds total                                       ║
║                                                                       ║
║  WHAT MUST HAVE UNIT TESTS:                                          ║
║  → LeaseBusinessRules.validate_rent_amount()                        ║
║  → LeaseBusinessRules.calculate_late_fee()                          ║
║  → LeaseBusinessRules.validate_lease_dates()                        ║
║  → FileUploadSecurity.validate()                                    ║
║  → Sanitizer.escapeHTML()                                           ║
║  → Sanitizer.safeURL()                                              ║
║  → Every serializer's validate_<field> method                      ║
║  → Every permission class (IsLandlord, IsPropertyOwner)            ║
║                                                                       ║
║  INTEGRATION TESTS (MANDATORY):                                      ║
║                                                                       ║
║  → Test every API endpoint (CRUD operations)                        ║
║  → Test authentication and authorization                            ║
║  → Test IDOR prevention (try to access other landlord's data)      ║
║  → Test rate limiting                                               ║
║  → Test Celery tasks (invoice generation, late fees)               ║
║  → Test WebSocket connections (Chat)                                ║
║  → Use test database (separate from dev DB)                        ║
║  → Use Django TestCase or pytest-django                             ║
║                                                                       ║
║  SECURITY TESTS (MANDATORY):                                         ║
║                                                                       ║
║  → SQL injection attempts on every filter/search input             ║
║  → XSS attempts on every text input field                          ║
║  → CSRF: verify POST without token is rejected                     ║
║  → Authentication bypass attempts                                   ║
║  → IDOR: access other landlord's resources by ID                   ║
║  → File upload: malicious files (PHP renamed to PDF, etc.)         ║
║  → Rate limiting: verify 429 after limit exceeded                  ║
║  → JWT: expired token, tampered token, missing token               ║
║                                                                       ║
║  TEST COVERAGE TARGETS:                                              ║
║  → Business logic (business_rules.py): 100%                        ║
║  → Security controls: 100%                                          ║
║  → API endpoints: 90%+                                              ║
║  → Template rendering: 70%+                                         ║
║  → Overall: 80%+ line coverage                                      ║
║                                                                       ║
║  TESTING TOOLS:                                                      ║
║  → pytest + pytest-django        (test runner)                     ║
║  → pytest-cov                    (coverage reporting)              ║
║  → factory_boy                   (test data factories)             ║
║  → responses                     (mock HTTP requests)              ║
║  → freezegun                     (mock datetime for date tests)    ║
║  → channels.testing              (WebSocket testing)               ║
║                                                                       ║

# 📊 PART 5: WELL-DEVELOPED SYSTEM STANDARDS

## 5.1 API Design Standards

```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║  API DESIGN STANDARDS                                                 ║
║  Reference: REST API Design — Roy Fielding, Stripe API Guidelines   ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                       ║
║  URL DESIGN:                                                         ║
║  → Use nouns not verbs: /api/v1/leases/ not /api/v1/get-leases/   ║
║  → Use plural: /api/v1/properties/ not /property/                  ║
║  → Hierarchy: /api/v1/properties/{id}/leases/                      ║
║  → Version in URL: /api/v1/ (allows non-breaking evolution)        ║
║  → Lowercase with hyphens: /api/v1/maintenance-tickets/            ║
║                                                                       ║
║  HTTP METHODS:                                                       ║
║  → GET:    Read (never modifies data)                               ║
║  → POST:   Create new resource                                      ║
║  → PUT:    Replace entire resource                                  ║
║  → PATCH:  Partial update (prefer over PUT)                        ║
║  → DELETE: Remove resource (soft delete in our system)             ║
║                                                                       ║
║  HTTP STATUS CODES:                                                  ║
║  → 200 OK:          Successful GET, PATCH, DELETE                  ║
║  → 201 Created:     Successful POST (new resource created)         ║
║  → 204 No Content:  Successful DELETE (no body returned)           ║
║  → 400 Bad Request: Validation error (return field errors)         ║
║  → 401 Unauthorized:Not authenticated (missing/expired token)      ║
║  → 403 Forbidden:   Authenticated but not authorized               ║
║  → 404 Not Found:   Resource not found OR IDOR protection          ║
║  → 409 Conflict:    Business rule conflict (lease overlap)         ║
║  → 422 Unprocessable:Business rule violation                       ║
║  → 429 Too Many:    Rate limit exceeded                             ║
║  → 500 Server Error:Unexpected error (no details exposed)          ║
║                                                                       ║
║  RESPONSE FORMAT:                                                    ║
║                                                                       ║
║  SUCCESS (list):                                                     ║
║  { "data": [...], "total": 25, "page": 1, "per_page": 25 }        ║
║                                                                       ║
║  SUCCESS (single):                                                   ║
║  { "data": { "id": "...", "name": "..." } }                        ║
║                                                                       ║
║  ERROR:                                                              ║
║  { "errors": { "field": ["error message"] } }                       ║
║  { "error": "Human-readable message" }                              ║
║                                                                       ║
║  WHAT NEVER APPEARS IN RESPONSE:                                     ║
║  → Stack traces                                                     ║
║  → Database error messages                                          ║
║  → Internal file paths                                              ║
║  → Server version or framework details                              ║
║  → Other users' data                                                ║
║                                                                       ║
║  API VERSIONING POLICY:                                              ║
║  → v1: Current stable API                                           ║
║  → New version (v2): when breaking changes are needed              ║
║  → Old version deprecated: 6 months notice before removal          ║
║  → Both versions run simultaneously during transition              ║
║                                                                       ║
║  AI CHECK: Verify all endpoints return correct HTTP status codes    ║
║  AI CHECK: Verify no sensitive data in error responses              ║
║  AI CHECK: Verify API version in all URL patterns                   ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

## 5.2 Database Migration Standards

```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║  DATABASE MIGRATION STANDARDS                                         ║
║  Reference: "Evolutionary Database Design" — Martin Fowler          ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                       ║
║  MIGRATION RULES:                                                    ║
║                                                                       ║
║  RULE 1: EVERY SCHEMA CHANGE IS A MIGRATION                         ║
║  → Never modify DB schema directly (no manual ALTER TABLE)          ║
║  → Always: python manage.py makemigrations                          ║
║  → Always: python manage.py migrate                                 ║
║  → Migration files are committed to Git                             ║
║                                                                       ║
║  RULE 2: MIGRATIONS MUST BE REVERSIBLE                              ║
║  → Every migration has backward() method                            ║
║  → Test rolling back before deploying forward                       ║
║  → If irreversible (data migration): document WHY and backup first  ║
║                                                                       ║
║  RULE 3: BACKWARD COMPATIBLE CHANGES FIRST                          ║
║  → Adding column: add nullable first, populate, then add constraint ║
║  → Renaming column: add new column, migrate data, remove old       ║
║  → Removing column: remove from code first, then drop from DB      ║
║  → WHY: Zero-downtime deployments require DB/code compatibility    ║
║                                                                       ║
║  RULE 4: DATA MIGRATIONS SEPARATE FROM SCHEMA MIGRATIONS           ║
║  → Schema migration: changes table structure                        ║
║  → Data migration: transforms existing data                         ║
║  → Keep them separate for clarity and reversibility                 ║
║                                                                       ║
║  RULE 5: MIGRATION CHECKLIST BEFORE DEPLOY                          ║
║  → Backup database                                                  ║
║  → Test migration on staging                                        ║
║  → Verify rollback works                                            ║
║  → Check migration has no long-running locks                        ║
║  → Run migrate with --run-syncdb=False in production               ║
║  → Verify application works after migration                        ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

Here is the straight answer, then what was changed in the templates.
How many landlord “pages”?
Per docs/rent and lease ui design description.txt (Section 1: “THE 14 LANDLORD PAGES”), there are 14 landlord screens. Your app exposes 14 matching routes under /landlord/... — one template each.
The sidebar shows 14 links (each opens one of those pages) plus Sign out, which is not one of the 14 pages; it is an action (clear session / JWT and go to login). The design doc counts 14 pages, not sign-out.

Below is a landlord page-by-page reference from Section 1 of docs/rent and lease ui design description.txt, plus concise goal and systems notes (goal = business intent; systems = what typically backs that screen in your stack from the doc + codebase).

1. Dashboard (/landlord/dashboard/)
	
Purpose	Command center for portfolio financial and operational health.
Goal	Answer “How is my portfolio doing right now?” in one glance.
Systems	Django server-rendered views; MySQL metrics (leases, invoices, maintenance, etc.).
Features	Portfolio overview metrics; recent transaction feed; expiring lease alerts.
Functionalities	Occupied vs vacant units; expected vs actual monthly revenue; overdue rent and open maintenance counts; renew lease actions on expiring contracts.


2. Properties (/landlord/properties/)
	
Purpose	Digital catalog of physical assets (units/properties).
Goal	Maintain accurate inventory of rentable units and occupancy.
Systems	Django + MySQL (Property); landlord-scoped API (/api/v1/properties/).
Features	Property grid; add/edit/delete; occupancy badges.
Functionalities	Add address, unit, base rent; edit details; delete when vacant (blocked if active lease); leased vs vacant badges.


3. Leases (/landlord/leases/)
	
Purpose	Contract hub: agreements and tenant onboarding (invites).
Goal	Legally and operationally tie tenants to units with clear terms.
Systems	Django + MySQL (Lease, Invitation); DRF /api/v1/leases/.
Features	Lease table; create lease; overlap date validation.
Functionalities	Sortable lease list; create lease (unit, dates, rent); overlap validation; email invite to tenant account/signing.


4. Financials (/landlord/financials/)
	
Purpose	Accounting ledger: invoices, late fees, revenue reporting.
Goal	Cash visibility, collections, and audit trail.
Systems	Django + MySQL (Invoice, etc.); DRF /api/v1/financials/.
Features	Invoice ledger; late-fee highlighting; revenue export.
Functionalities	Filter by property, month, status; base rent + late fee (e.g. 5%) per row; CSV/PDF export; overdue row emphasis.


5. Chat (/landlord/chat/)
	
Purpose	Real-time messaging with assigned tenants (WhatsApp-style).
Goal	Fast, logged communication without leaving the CRM.
Systems	Django Channels + WebSockets (per architecture doc); Redis channel layer; JWT/session auth.
Features	Two-pane layout; tenant list; read receipts; typing indicators.
Functionalities	Pick tenant thread; send/receive over WebSockets; attachments; drag-and-drop files; read receipts; online/offline.


6. Maintenance (/landlord/maintenance/)
	
Purpose	Workflow for repair requests (Kanban).
Goal	Clear pipeline from request to resolution.
Systems	Django + MySQL (MaintenanceTicket); optional API when wired.
Features	Three columns; drag-and-drop; priority tags.
Functionalities	Pending / in progress / resolved; drag to change status; ticket detail with photos; priority (e.g. emergency vs low).


7. Tenants (/landlord/tenants/)
	
Purpose	CRM-style directory of tenant relationships.
Goal	Human-centric view of who rents from you and how to act.
Systems	Django + MySQL (leases → tenant users); optional APIs for enrichment.
Features	Searchable list; slide-out detail; message routing.
Functionalities	Active vs moved-out filters; row opens drawer; emergency contacts, payment history, tickets; “Message tenant” → Chat.


8. Documents (/landlord/documents/)
	
Purpose	Secure vault for legal/property/tenant files.
Goal	One compliant place for contracts and evidence.
Systems	Django file storage; JWT-protected download; IDOR middleware patterns from doc.
Features	Drag-and-drop upload; folder grid; secure download.
Functionalities	Upload PDFs/images; folders per property; authenticated download; typed DELETE confirmation.


9. Analytics (/landlord/analytics/)
	
Purpose	Turn DB records into charts and decisions.
Goal	Trend and mix analysis beyond raw tables.
Systems	Django + MySQL aggregates; Chart.js (per doc and current templates).
Features	12-month revenue line; maintenance donut; payment timeliness donut.
Functionalities	Chart.js trends; category breakdown; on-time vs late; CSV export of analytics report.


10. Notifications (/landlord/notifications/)
	
Purpose	Chronological audit feed of system events.
Goal	Nothing critical is missed (payments, fees, tickets, chat).
Systems	Django + notification store (model/API when implemented); pagination.
Features	Feed; read/unread; icon-coded types.
Functionalities	Reverse chronological order; mark all read; paginate older; color icons (payments, late fees, tickets, chat).


11. Settings (/landlord/settings/)
	
Purpose	Account, security, bank, and notification preferences.
Goal	Correct profile and payout configuration.
Systems	Django auth user; forms to user/profile APIs when built.
Features	Vertical tabs; profile, security, bank forms; toggles.
Functionalities	Update name/phone; change password; bank/receiving details; per-email notification toggles.


12. Expenses (/landlord/expenses/)
	
Purpose	Expense log and net ROI vs rent collected.
Goal	True net performance per property/portfolio.
Systems	Django + MySQL expense/ledger models when implemented; ties to financials.
Features	Expense log; net income widget; offline payment recording.
Functionalities	Log costs (repairs, taxes, etc.); record offline cash; auto net rent minus expenses; per-property net view.


13. Buildings (/landlord/buildings/)
	
Purpose	Group units under parent buildings (hierarchy).
Goal	Scale UI and reporting for multi-unit portfolios.
Systems	Django + MySQL (Building, Property linkage).
Features	Parent buildings; tree/accordion; bulk views.
Functionalities	Create building; assign units; expand/collapse units; aggregate financials per building.


14. Reminder (/landlord/automations/ — sidebar label Reminder)
	
Purpose	Control panel for scheduled reminders and fee/lease automations (doc: “Automated Reminders Control Panel”).
Goal	Reduce manual follow-ups and standardize policy (reminders, late fees, expiry warnings).
Systems	Django + Celery/beat (per project settings); API toggles to persist automation flags.
Features	Cron-style toggles; live status; descriptions per job.
Functionalities	Toggle e.g. 3-day rent reminder emails; auto 5% late fee; 60-day lease expiry warning; reflect active/inactive; API updates backend jobs.
